`st_centroid()` returns the **center of mass** — the balance point of the shape - Used for: distance calculations, representative points, labeling ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} luzern_centroid <- st_centroid(luzern) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](geometry-operations_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## - For **concave** or **C-shaped** geometries, the centroid can fall **outside** the polygon - `st_point_on_surface()` always returns a point **inside** - Typical uses: - `st_centroid()`: Distance metrics, spatial analytics - `st_point_on_surface()`: Map labeling, feature sampling ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](geometry-operations_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: # Affine Transformations {.subtitle} ## Three elementary operations - **Affine transformations** preserve lines and parallelism — angles and lengths may change - In `sf`: applied directly to `sfc` objects using arithmetic operators | Operation | sf syntax | Effect | |---|---|---| | Shift | `sfc + c(dx, dy)` | Move without changing shape | | Scale | `(sfc - p) * factor + p` | Grow or shrink around a point `p` | | Rotate | `(sfc - p) * R(θ) + center` | Rotate around a point `p` | :::{.notes} The pattern `(sfc - center) * operation + center` appears in both scale and rotate: subtract center to bring the geometry to the origin, apply the transformation, then shift back. This is the key insight students should take away. ::: ## Shift and Scale ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Shift: move 10 km east luzern_shifted <- luzern_sfc + c(10000, 0) # Scale: shrink to 75% around centroid luzern_scaled <- (luzern_sfc - luzern_center) * 0.75 + luzern_center ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](geometry-operations_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Rotation - **Shift to origin → rotate → shift back** — otherwise the geometry rotates around (0, 0) - $R(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rotation <- function(deg) { r <- deg * pi / 180 # convert degrees to radians matrix( # c(cos(r), -sin(r), # [ cos(r), -sin(r) ] sin(r), cos(r)), # [ sin(r), cos(r) ] nrow = 2, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE ) } ``` ::: --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} luzern_rotated <- (luzern_sfc - luzern_center) * rotation(15) + luzern_center ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](geometry-operations_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: --- The same pattern applies to all three operations — only the transformation differs: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} (sfc - center) + center # identity (no-op) (sfc - center) * 0.5 + center # scale (sfc - center) * rotation(45) + center # rotate ``` ::: Transformations **compose**: shift first, then scale, then rotate gives a different result than the reverse order. # Simplification {.subtitle} ## Why simplify? - Real datasets carry more vertices than any display scale needs - Excess vertices: slow rendering, large files, no visual benefit ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](geometry-operations_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Challenge: Line simplification Algorithm - **Given:** a polyline V₁, V₂, ..., Vₙ - **Task:** develop an algorithm that removes "unnecessary" vertices — those that add no meaningful shape information at scale ε :::{.callout-important title="Closed book!"} Do not use any external sources. Solve with your own ideas in groups ::: ## Douglas-Peucker - `st_simplify()` uses the **Douglas-Peucker** algorithm - Core idea: a point is **unnecessary** if it lies close to the line between its neighbours - Tolerance ε controls how much deviation is acceptable :::{.r-stack} ![Step 1: draw baseline from first to last point](images/douglas-peucker-1.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out width="80%"} ![Step 2: find the farthest point — distance d = 3 > ε → keep it](images/douglas-peucker-2.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out width="80%"} ![Step 3: recurse on both halves independently](images/douglas-peucker-3.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out width="80%"} ![Step 4: continue recursion — more points kept or discarded](images/douglas-peucker-4.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out width="80%"} ![Step 5: result — only the essential vertices remain (blue)](images/douglas-peucker-5.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out width="80%"} ::: ## The topology problem - `st_simplify()` processes each feature **independently** - Shared boundaries are simplified separately → **gaps and overlaps** appear ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](geometry-operations_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Topology-preserving simplification - `rmapshaper::ms_simplify()` simplifies the **whole layer at once** — shared boundaries stay consistent - Uses the **Visvalingam** algorithm: iteratively removes the vertex that creates the smallest triangle area ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(rmapshaper) # We specify the proportion of points to keep n_ms <- ms_simplify(neighbors, keep = 0.5) ``` ::: --- ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](geometry-operations_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Summary - **`st_centroid()`** returns the geometric centre of mass — useful for distance calculations and analytics, but it can fall *outside* the shape for concave or C-shaped geometries. Use **`st_point_on_surface()`** when you need a point guaranteed to lie inside. - **Affine transformations** (shift, scale, rotate) preserve shape and angles. All three follow the same pattern in sf: shift to the origin, apply the transformation, shift back. sf lets you do this with ordinary arithmetic directly on `sfc` objects. Transformations are not commutative — order matters. - **`st_simplify()`** reduces vertex count using the Douglas-Peucker algorithm: it recursively removes vertices that deviate less than tolerance ε from the local baseline. It operates feature by feature, so shared boundaries between adjacent polygons can develop gaps and overlaps. - **`ms_simplify()`** (rmapshaper) uses the Visvalingam algorithm and processes the entire layer at once, keeping shared edges consistent. Prefer it whenever topology matters.

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
